channel.title: Enduring
channel.description: Enduring tells the stories hiding behind the things that last. Every episode takes a name you might recognize, a famous product or a quietly unstoppable business, and digs into the real company behind it. The fires survived, the near-death moments, the families who kept the doors open for a hundred years. This channel is for entertainment and curiosity only.

item.title: TABASCO: Made on One Island Since 1868
item.description:
A little bottle with a diamond label and a red cap that teaches you how to use it — two drops. It's on tables in 195 countries, but it's still made on one hill in Louisiana where the seed stock is kept, the barrels are aged, and the blending happens.
How Edmund McIlhenny turned a garden experiment into 658 bottles in 1869, why the first bottles were cologne bottles, how a CAUTION notice — "One or two drops are enough for a plate of soup, meat, oysters, and more, one bottle being equal to a dozen of the ordinary kind" — became necessary, why Tabasco and oysters became a pair, how John McIlhenny's Rough Riders and Edward's Bird City and Jungle Gardens shaped the island, how Walter McIlhenny's Marine rations turned into a cookbook and then MRE packets, why the family spent $5 million on a 17-foot levee after Rita in 2005 instead of moving, and how 50 years of trademark fights turned a Mexican state name into one company's name in the US.
Three ingredients. Up to three years in oak. One place responsible for the final result.
This show is for entertainment and curiosity only. Nothing you hear on Enduring is investment advice, financial advice, or a recommendation to buy or sell anything.

item.title: Kikkoman: The 350-Year-Old Bottle in Your Fridge
item.description: A wide-bottom bottle with a red cap and a dripless spout that hasn't changed since 1961 — because it didn't need to. It's in most American supermarkets and many western kitchens, but the company behind it has been brewing since 1661 in Noda, Japan. How the Mogi family built a soy sauce town, why the name Kikkoman — hexagon, tortoise shell, ten thousand years — was first used in 1782, how eight brewers merged in 1917 to survive, how Yuzaburo Mogi taught America to cook with soy sauce instead of just pouring it, why Walworth, Wisconsin became the first major factory built by a Japanese company in the US in 1973, and how designer Kenji Ekuan's bottle made it into the Museum of Modern Art. Soybeans, wheat, salt, water, koji. Six months. This show is for entertainment and curiosity only. Nothing you hear on Enduring is investment advice, financial advice, or a recommendation to buy or sell anything. We do one lasting company at a time, fifteen to twenty minutes, no hype.
item.itunes:author: Enduring

item.title: Lena Blackburne: The Secret Mud Behind Every Baseball
item.description: Every Major League Baseball used this season was rubbed with the same thing — not a machine, not a factory, but a handful of mud from a secret spot on the Delaware River in New Jersey that only six people outside one family are allowed to know about. How Lena Blackburne found it in 1938, why nothing else works without darkening the ball, and why the smallest supplier in baseball still has a full-time printing press job. From Ray Chapman in 1920 and the end of the dead-ball era to a thousand pounds a year, ten pounds per team, and the experiments that still can't replace it. This show is for entertainment and curiosity only. Nothing you hear on Enduring is investment advice, financial advice, or a recommendation to buy or sell anything. We do one lasting company at a time, fifteen to twenty minutes, no hype.
item.itunes:author: Enduring

item.title: LEGO: The Perfect Brick and the Company That Nearly Lost It
item.description: A carpenter in Billund, three fires, a borrowed brick, and a tolerance of ten microns. How LEGO became the world's default building system, nearly innovated itself out of existence in 2003, and rebuilt by remembering that yesterday, today and tomorrow must connect.
item.itunes:author: Enduring

item.title: The Company That Prints Money (But Isn't Allowed to Say Whose)
item.description: A two-hundred-year-old printer from Guernsey that became the world's largest commercial banknote maker — for over a hundred countries, 40+ central banks, 7 billion notes a year — and must never put its name on the product. Wars, cash machines, polymer, and why secrecy is the product.
item.itunes:author: Enduring

item.title: EP03: LOWA
item.description: A century of Bavarian bootmaking: three cobbler brothers who each founded a famous boot company, a brass band that paid for the first machines, war and denazification, a near-collapse in the nineties, and the Italian deal that kept the doors open. This show is for entertainment and curiosity only.
item.itunes:author: Enduring

item.title: EP02: YKK
item.description: Ninety-two years, one founding family, and roughly half the zippers on Earth. The story of how a small Tokyo workshop beat the zipper's American inventors, built the machines that make the machines, and grew a business most people have never heard of. This show is for entertainment and curiosity only.
item.itunes:author: Enduring

item.title: EP01: Lodge Cast Iron
item.description: The 130-year-old Tennessee company behind America's most famous skillet: a teenage founder who walked 1,200 miles, the fire that burned it all down, the garden gnomes that saved the Great Depression, and the invention of pre-seasoned cast iron. This show is for entertainment and curiosity only, and nothing here is investment advice.
